title: Stacks and Queues
description: Understand stacks (LIFO) and queues (FIFO), their implementations, and where each structure appears in real systems.

data.text: Stacks and queues are abstract data types that enforce a specific order of operations. A stack removes the most recently added item first (Last In, First Out), while a queue removes the oldest item first (First In, First Out). These simple rules make them powerful building blocks for larger systems.
A stack supports two primary operations: push, which places an item on top, and pop, which removes the top item. A peek operation lets you inspect the top item without removing it.

data.title: Stack operations
items: push(item) — add an item to the top.
pop() — remove and return the top item.
peek() — view the top item without removing it.
isEmpty() — check whether the stack contains items.

data.title: Stack in JavaScript
data.content: A minimal stack built on an array. Stacks are easy to implement because arrays already provide push and pop.

data.text: A queue supports enqueue, which adds an item to the back, and dequeue, which removes the item from the front. A peek operation returns the front item without removing it.

data.title: Queue operations
items: enqueue(item) — add an item to the back.
dequeue() — remove and return the front item.
peek() — view the front item without removing it.
isEmpty() — check whether the queue contains items.

data.title: Queue in JavaScript
data.content: A queue implemented with an array. For high throughput, a linked list or circular buffer is preferred because shifting elements is expensive.

rows: Most recent change should reverse first
Pages visited are popped in reverse order
Jobs should print in arrival order

data.text: A priority queue assigns a priority to each item. The item with the highest priority leaves first, regardless of insertion order. A heap is the most efficient underlying implementation because insertion and extraction both run in O(log n) time.

data.title: Performance note
data.text: Array-based queues that use shift() or unshift() can degrade to O(n) per operation. For large workloads, prefer a linked list or a ring buffer. For priority ordering, reach for a heap.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Stacks are LIFO: last item added is removed first.
Queues are FIFO: first item added is removed first.
Both structures are foundational for algorithms such as BFS and undo systems.
Choose an implementation that matches your throughput and memory requirements.
data.takeaway: Stacks and queues are everywhere in software because they model order naturally.
